scenarios.title: Ending Manual Deploys at Chitra Prints
scenarios.background: Chitra Prints is a fictional online photo-printing startup in Jaipur. Its Python web app is deployed by one developer who copies files to the server over FTP late at night. Tests exist but are run only when someone remembers, and bugs reach customers regularly. A new hire's code works on her laptop but fails on the server because the Python and library versions differ. The founders want deploys to become routine and safe.
constraints: The team is four developers, none dedicated to operations
The app runs on a single Linux server today
Customers order prints around the clock

questions.prompt: Tests are run only when someone remembers, so bugs reach customers. What is the first practice to introduce?

options.text: Ask everyone to promise that they will run the tests before deploying
Run the tests on every push and block merging when they fail
Run the full test suite once a month, on the last Friday of it
Delete the tests that fail most often, since they slow down work

questions.explanation: Continuous integration runs the test suite automatically on every push or pull request, so a broken change is caught within minutes. Blocking merges when tests fail stops broken code from reaching the main branch, without relying on anyone remembering.

why_others_wrong.a: Promises fail under deadline pressure; automation does not forget.
why_others_wrong.c: A month of changes piles up between runs, so failures are hard to trace and fix.
why_others_wrong.d: Deleting failing tests hides problems instead of fixing them.

questions.key_justification: Automate tests on every change and gate merges on the result.

questions.prompt: Code works on the new developer's laptop but fails on the server because the Python and library versions differ. What solves this best?

options.text: Give every developer the same laptop model and operating system
Write a wiki page listing which Python version to install by hand
Package the app and its pinned dependencies as a container image
Update the server's libraries to the newest versions every week

questions.explanation: A container image bundles the app with the exact runtime and library versions it needs, so the same image runs identically on a laptop, in CI and on the server. Pinning dependency versions in the build keeps those environments matched over time.

why_others_wrong.a: Identical laptops still drift as people install different packages, and the server is not a laptop.
why_others_wrong.b: Manual setup instructions are followed inconsistently and go out of date.
why_others_wrong.d: Unplanned weekly upgrades create new differences and can break the app without warning.

questions.key_justification: Containers with pinned dependencies make environments consistent from laptop to production.

questions.prompt: Which two practices belong in a good Dockerfile for this Python app?

options.text: Start from a small base image with a pinned version tag
Copy the payment API key into the image during the build
Install dependencies before copying code, to reuse layers
Always use the 'latest' tag so the base stays up to date
Run the app as the root user so it never hits permissions

questions.explanation: A small, pinned base image such as python:3.12-slim keeps the image lean and builds repeatable. Copying the requirements file and installing dependencies before copying the code means Docker reuses the cached dependency layer when only the code changes, which makes builds much faster.

why_others_wrong.b: Secrets baked into an image can be read by anyone who pulls it; they should be injected at runtime.
why_others_wrong.d: 'latest' changes without warning, so the same Dockerfile can produce different images.
why_others_wrong.e: Running as root means any break-in gets full control of the container.

questions.key_justification: Pin small base images, order layers for caching, and keep secrets and root out of images.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

targets.text: Keeping every change in a state ready to release at any time
A store of versioned build outputs, such as images or packages
Merging and testing changes often, automatically, into one branch
A packaged app with its runtime and libraries, ready to run

questions.explanation: Continuous integration merges and tests changes frequently and automatically. Continuous delivery keeps the result always releasable, so a deploy is a routine decision, a container image packages the app with what it needs to run, and an artifact registry stores versioned builds for deployment.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Treating continuous delivery as automatic deployment of every change to production: that is continuous deployment, while delivery means every change is ready to release when the team chooses.

questions.key_justification: CI, CD, images and registries are the core building blocks of a delivery pipeline.

scenarios.title: Designing the Release Process at Swaad Kitchens
scenarios.background: Swaad Kitchens is a fictional cloud-kitchen brand in Bengaluru with 40 kitchens and an ordering platform built by 15 developers. Feature branches live for weeks and merging them is painful. Deploys happen on Friday nights with 20 minutes of downtime, staging and production are built separately from different branches, and rolling back takes hours. Lunch and dinner peaks mean any outage loses real orders.
constraints: There must be no downtime during lunch and dinner peaks
A bad release must be reversible within minutes
Fifteen developers work in the same repository

questions.prompt: Feature branches live for weeks, and merging them causes days of conflicts. What branching approach should the team move to?

options.text: Make the feature branches last even longer, so merges are rarer
Short-lived branches merged daily, unfinished work behind flags
One branch per developer that is merged only at each quarter's end
Everyone edits the production server's files directly, no branches

questions.explanation: Trunk-based development keeps branches small and merges them into the main branch at least daily, so conflicts stay tiny and are resolved while fresh. Feature flags let unfinished features be merged and deployed while still switched off for customers.

why_others_wrong.a: Longer branches drift further apart, so the eventual merge gets worse, not better.
why_others_wrong.c: Quarterly merges create huge, risky integrations, the opposite of what is needed.
why_others_wrong.d: Editing production directly removes review, testing and history.

questions.key_justification: Integrate small changes frequently and hide unfinished work behind feature flags.

questions.prompt: Deploys cause 20 minutes of downtime, and rollback takes hours. Which deployment strategy fixes both?

options.text: Stop the old version, then start the new one in its place
Deploy only at 3 am so fewer customers notice the downtime
Run the new version alongside the old and switch the traffic
Copy the new files over the old ones while the app is running

questions.explanation: In a blue-green deployment the new version is started and checked next to the old one, and traffic is then switched to it at the load balancer, with no downtime. If something goes wrong, switching traffic back to the old version takes seconds.

why_others_wrong.a: This is the current approach, which causes the downtime.
why_others_wrong.b: Kitchens take orders around the clock, and a 3 am deploy still means downtime and slow rollback.
why_others_wrong.d: Overwriting live files can leave the app half old and half new, and gives no easy way back.

questions.key_justification: Blue-green deployment gives zero-downtime switches and near-instant rollback.

questions.prompt: A risky change to the order-pricing logic is ready. How should it be released?

options.text: Send 5% of traffic to it, compare errors, and roll back if worse
Release to all 40 kitchens at once to get it over with quickly
Release it without any monitoring, so the dashboards stay quiet
Hold it back until every possible bug has been found in testing

questions.explanation: A canary release sends a small share of real traffic to the new version and compares its error rate and key metrics, such as order values, with the old version. If the canary looks worse, it is rolled back automatically before most customers are affected.

why_others_wrong.b: A pricing bug would then hit every order across every kitchen at the same time.
why_others_wrong.c: Without monitoring, nobody would know the change was hurting orders.
why_others_wrong.d: No amount of testing finds every bug, so waiting for certainty means never releasing.

questions.key_justification: Canary releases limit the impact of risky changes and allow evidence-based rollback.

questions.prompt: Staging and production are built separately from different branches, so they behave differently. Which two practices fix this?

options.text: Build one image per commit, tagged by SHA, promoted to each env
Rebuild the app separately for each environment from its branch
Inject environment settings at deploy time, not at build time
Edit configuration on the production servers by hand when needed
Use the 'latest' image tag in production so it is always fresh

questions.explanation: Building once and promoting the identical image through staging to production means production runs exactly what was tested. Settings that differ, such as database addresses, are supplied when the image is deployed, so the image itself never changes between environments.

why_others_wrong.b: Separate builds can pick up different code or dependencies, so staging no longer proves anything.
why_others_wrong.d: Hand edits are untracked, easily forgotten and cause environments to drift apart.
why_others_wrong.e: 'latest' hides which version is running and can change underneath a deployment.

questions.key_justification: Build an artifact once and promote it unchanged, with configuration injected per environment.

questions.prompt: Match each release problem to the practice that solves it.

items.text: Only one person knows the deploy steps, and does them by hand
Production settings drift away from staging without anyone noticing
Nobody can tell which version is running in production right now
Rolling back a bad release takes several hours

targets.text: Report the build's commit SHA from a health endpoint
Keep the previous artifact and roll back with one command
Store all configuration in version control and review it
An automated pipeline that anyone on the team can run

questions.explanation: Automating the deploy removes the dependence on one person. Versioned, reviewed configuration stops silent drift, exposing the build's commit SHA shows exactly what is running, and keeping the previous artifact ready turns rollback into a single quick step.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Fixing the single-person problem with a written checklist: a checklist still needs someone to run every step by hand, while a pipeline makes the deploy repeatable for anyone.

questions.key_justification: Automation, versioned config, visible versions and ready rollbacks make releases routine.

code_pool.prompt: With releases cut from main many times a week, Swaad Kitchens wants version numbers worked out from the commit messages (Conventional Commits) instead of argued about. The first line is the current version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, the second is n, then n commit messages. Complete `next_version`: a message containing `BREAKING CHANGE`, or whose type ends in `!` before the colon (like `feat!: ...`), means a major release; otherwise any message starting with `feat` means minor; otherwise any starting with `fix` means patch. A major bump resets minor and patch to 0, a minor bump resets patch. Print the new version, or `no release`.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def next_version(current, messages):
    """current: 'MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH'. messages: commit messages since that release. A message containing 'BREAKING CHANGE', or whose type ends in '!' before the ':' (like 'feat!:'), is a major bump; else any message starting 'feat' is minor; else any starting 'fix' is patch. Return the new version, or 'no release'."""
    # Write your code here.
    return current


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    current = data[0].strip()
    n = int(data[1])
    print(next_version(current, data[2:2 + n]))


main()
code_pool.explanation: The release level is the strongest change among the commits, so one pass keeps the maximum. Semantic versioning then tells other teams something useful: a major number change warns them an API broke. Parsing the numbers as integers matters: 1.9.0 then 1.10.0, not 1.9.1.
code_pool.key_justification: Parse version strings and commit prefixes; keep the highest bump.

code_pool.reference_solution:
import sys


def canary_decision(minutes):
    """minutes: list of (baseline requests, baseline errors, canary requests, canary errors) per minute; baseline requests are always > 0. Using running totals, from the first minute the canary has served at least 100 requests: if its error rate is above 2 x the baseline rate + 1 percentage point, return 'ROLLBACK at minute m'. Otherwise return 'PROMOTE', or 'WAIT' if the canary never reached 100 requests."""
    rb = eb = rc = ec = 0
    for minute, (b_req, b_err, c_req, c_err) in enumerate(minutes, 1):
        rb, eb, rc, ec = rb + b_req, eb + b_err, rc + c_req, ec + c_err
        # ec/rc > 2*eb/rb + 1/100   <=>   100*ec*rb > 200*eb*rc + rb*rc   (all counts positive)
        if rc >= 100 and 100 * ec * rb > 200 * eb * rc + rb * rc:
            return f"ROLLBACK at minute {minute}"
    return "PROMOTE" if rc >= 100 else "WAIT"


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    minutes = [tuple(map(int, data[1 + i].split())) for i in range(n)]
    print(canary_decision(minutes))


main()
code_pool.explanation: Running totals over the minutes give the cumulative error rates; waiting for 100 canary requests avoids judging on a handful of calls. Comparing against the baseline at the same time separates a bad release from a bad hour. Cross-multiplying keeps the comparison exact.
code_pool.key_justification: Cumulative rates over an array with an exact integer comparison.

scenarios.title: Untangling the Pipeline at Rail Yatra Info
scenarios.background: Rail Yatra Info is a fictional train-status service in Lucknow running on Kubernetes. Developers complain that the CI pipeline takes 45 minutes and that one test fails randomly about one run in ten, so they just press 'rerun'. In production, a newly deployed service keeps restarting, another is repeatedly killed for using too much memory, and a deploy that 'succeeded' never received any traffic.
constraints: Train-status data must stay available during festival travel
Twelve developers wait on the pipeline before each merge
The cluster runs on a managed Kubernetes service

questions.prompt: One test fails randomly about one run in ten, and developers just rerun the pipeline. What should the team do?

options.text: Keep rerunning until it passes, since it passes most of the time
Quarantine the test, find what makes it flaky, and fix the cause
Set the pipeline to retry every test ten times before it can fail
Turn off the whole test suite until the flaky test fixes itself

questions.explanation: Flaky tests teach people to ignore red builds, so real failures slip through. Moving the test out of the blocking suite while it is investigated keeps the pipeline trustworthy, and its usual causes, such as dependence on time, test order or shared state, can then be found and fixed.

why_others_wrong.a: Constant reruns waste time and train the team to ignore failures.
why_others_wrong.c: Blanket retries hide flakiness everywhere and can mask real intermittent bugs.
why_others_wrong.d: Disabling all tests removes the safety net completely.

questions.key_justification: Quarantine and fix flaky tests instead of normalising reruns.

questions.prompt: A new pod keeps restarting and shows CrashLoopBackOff. What is the best first step?

options.text: Delete the cluster and create a new one from scratch right away
Raise the replica count so some pods stay up between the crashes
Read the crashed container's logs and the pod's recent events
Turn off the restart policy so that the pod stops restarting

questions.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts, exits and is restarted again and again. Its own output, for example from kubectl logs with the --previous flag, plus the pod's events from kubectl describe, usually show the reason, such as a missing environment variable or a failed connection.

why_others_wrong.a: The cluster is not the problem; rebuilding it loses time and changes nothing about the app.
why_others_wrong.b: More replicas means more crashing copies, not a fix.
why_others_wrong.d: Stopping restarts leaves the service down and still hides why it crashes.

questions.key_justification: Diagnose crash loops from the failed container's logs and the pod's events.

questions.prompt: The pipeline takes 45 minutes: 15 to download dependencies and 30 to run tests one after another. What helps most?

options.text: Cache dependencies between runs and split tests to run in parallel
Delete half the tests, choosing them at random, to save some time
Run the pipeline only on Fridays, so it runs less often overall
Buy faster laptops for developers and leave the pipeline as it is

questions.explanation: Caching dependencies, keyed on the lock file, avoids downloading the same packages on every run. Splitting the test suite across several parallel jobs cuts the 30-minute stage roughly by the number of jobs, so feedback arrives in minutes.

why_others_wrong.b: Random deletion removes protection without targeting what is slow.
why_others_wrong.c: Running rarely means changes go unchecked and problems pile up.
why_others_wrong.d: The pipeline runs on CI machines, so laptops do not change its duration.

questions.key_justification: Speed up pipelines by caching dependencies and parallelising tests.

questions.prompt: A service is repeatedly killed with OOMKilled. Which two steps should the team take?

options.text: Compare the container's memory limit with its measured usage
Delete the namespace and redeploy everything in it from scratch
Fix the memory growth, or set a limit that fits real needs
Disable the health checks so Kubernetes stops killing the pods
Remove memory limits from every container in the cluster

questions.explanation: OOMKilled means the container used more memory than its limit allowed. Comparing usage metrics with the limit shows whether the limit is simply too low for normal load or whether memory grows without end, which points to a leak that must be fixed in the code.

why_others_wrong.b: Redeploying the same code with the same limit reproduces the same kills.
why_others_wrong.d: The kill comes from the memory limit, not from health checks, so disabling them changes nothing.
why_others_wrong.e: Without limits, one leaking container can starve every other workload on the node.

questions.key_justification: Resolve OOM kills by comparing limits with real usage and fixing leaks or sizing correctly.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom to its most likely cause.

items.text: A deploy 'succeeded', but the new pods never receive any traffic
The service works in staging but fails in production with 'host not found'
Builds fail with 'no space left on device' on the build agent
Pods are restarted in the middle of serving slow requests

targets.text: Old images and build caches are never cleaned up
The liveness probe's timeout is too aggressive
The readiness probe keeps failing for the new pods
A production setting or secret is missing or wrong

questions.explanation: Kubernetes sends traffic only to pods whose readiness probe passes, so pods that never become ready get none. 'Host not found' in only one environment points to that environment's configuration, a full build disk usually comes from images and caches that are never cleaned, and a liveness probe with too short a timeout restarts pods that are merely busy.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Mixing up the two probes: a failing readiness probe removes a pod from traffic, while a failing liveness probe restarts the container.

questions.key_justification: Probe types, environment config and agent hygiene explain common deployment symptoms.

code_pool.prompt: One test fails about one run in ten and developers just press rerun. Find the flaky tests from CI history. The first line is n, then n lines `commit test result` (PASS or FAIL). Complete `find_flaky`: a test is flaky if it both passed and failed on the same commit (the code did not change, yet the result did). A test that fails on one commit and passes on a later one is not flaky; it was fixed. The program prints `test rate%` (the test's fail rate over all its runs, rounded down) for each flaky test, sorted by name, or NONE.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def find_flaky(runs):
    """runs: list of (commit, test, PASS or FAIL). A test is flaky if it both passed and failed on the SAME commit. Return [(test, fail rate over all its runs as a whole percent rounded down)] sorted by test."""
    # Write your code here.
    return []


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    runs = [tuple(data[1 + i].split()) for i in range(n)]
    flaky = find_flaky(runs)
    if not flaky:
        print("NONE")
    for test, rate in flaky:
        print(test, f"{rate}%")


main()
code_pool.explanation: Grouping results by (test, commit) in a dictionary of sets shows whether one unchanged commit produced both outcomes, which is the definition of flaky. Rerunning hides the problem and teaches the team to ignore red builds; listing flaky tests with their fail rate lets them be quarantined and fixed.
code_pool.key_justification: Group results by (test, commit) to separate flaky from broken.

code_pool.prompt: The CI pipeline takes 45 minutes. Before buying faster machines, find out where the time goes when independent stages run in parallel. The first line is n, then n lines `stage minutes deps` (deps comma-separated, or -). Complete `earliest_schedule`, assuming unlimited runners: a stage starts as soon as all its prerequisites have finished (at minute 0 if it has none). The program prints `stage start finish` for every stage, sorted by name, then `total T`, the minute the whole pipeline finishes (the critical path).
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def earliest_schedule(stages):
    """stages: {name: (minutes, [stages it needs first])}, a DAG; unlimited runners. A stage starts when all its prerequisites have finished (at 0 if it has none). Return ([(name, start, finish)] sorted by name, the time the whole pipeline finishes)."""
    # Write your code here.
    return [], 0


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    stages = {}
    for i in range(n):
        name, minutes, deps = data[1 + i].split()
        stages[name] = (int(minutes), [] if deps == "-" else deps.split(","))
    schedule, total = earliest_schedule(stages)
    for name, start, finish in schedule:
        print(name, start, finish)
    print("total", total)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Each stage's earliest finish is its own duration plus the latest finish among its prerequisites, a longest-path calculation on the DAG done with memoised recursion. The total is the critical path: speeding up any stage off that path saves nothing, so this shows exactly which stages are worth optimising or splitting.
code_pool.key_justification: Longest path (critical path) in a DAG with memoisation.

scenarios.title: Reliability Budgets at Sampark Telecom
scenarios.background: Sampark Telecom is a fictional mobile operator in Kolkata whose self-service portal lets 8 million customers recharge and pay bills. Leadership has set an availability target of 99.9% per month for the portal, product teams want to ship weekly, and the on-call engineer receives about 200 alerts a week, most of which need no action. A small new team running two simple services is also asking whether it should adopt Kubernetes.
constraints: The portal's availability target is 99.9% over each 30-day month
The new team has three engineers and two services

questions.prompt: Roughly how much downtime does a 99.9% availability target allow over a 30-day month?

options.text: About 4 minutes
About 43 minutes
About 7 hours
About 3 days

questions.explanation: A 30-day month has 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is about 43 minutes. That allowance is the error budget: the amount of unreliability the team can 'spend' on incidents and risky releases before missing the target.

why_others_wrong.a: About 4 minutes a month matches a 99.99% target.
why_others_wrong.c: About 7 hours a month matches a 99% target.
why_others_wrong.d: Three days is roughly 10% downtime, a 90% availability target.

questions.key_justification: 99.9% of 43,200 minutes leaves about 43 minutes of allowed downtime.

questions.prompt: Halfway through the month, incidents have used the whole error budget. Under a typical error-budget policy, what should happen next?

options.text: Keep shipping weekly features, since the budget is only a guideline
Lower the target to 99% so the budget is no longer used up
Pause risky launches and put engineering effort on reliability
Stop all deployments, including urgent fixes, until next month

questions.explanation: An error budget makes the speed-versus-stability trade-off explicit. When it is spent, the agreed policy usually shifts effort to reliability work and holds risky feature launches until the service is stable again, while still allowing fixes that improve reliability.

why_others_wrong.a: Ignoring the budget makes the target meaningless and risks further outages.
why_others_wrong.b: Moving the target to hide the overspend defeats the purpose of having one.
why_others_wrong.d: Blocking urgent fixes can prolong incidents; reliability improvements should still ship.

questions.key_justification: When the error budget is spent, shift effort from features to reliability.

questions.prompt: A new team of three engineers runs two simple web services. Should it adopt Kubernetes now?

options.text: Yes, because every modern team is expected to run Kubernetes
Yes, and the team should run its own cluster on bare-metal servers
No; run each service on its own manually patched virtual machine
Not yet; a managed container platform gives most benefits for less

questions.explanation: Kubernetes is powerful but adds significant operational complexity. For two simple services, a managed container platform or PaaS provides deployment, scaling and health checks with far less to learn and maintain, and the team can move to Kubernetes later if its needs grow.

why_others_wrong.a: Popularity is not a reason to take on complexity a team does not need.
why_others_wrong.b: Self-hosting on bare metal adds even more operations work for three engineers.
why_others_wrong.c: Manually patched VMs bring back the toil and drift that containers avoid.

questions.key_justification: Choose the simplest platform that meets current needs; adopt Kubernetes when it pays off.

questions.prompt: The on-call engineer gets about 200 alerts a week, and most need no action. Which two changes help most?

options.text: Delete or tune the alerts that never lead to any action
Add more alerts so that no possible problem is ever missed
Page only for SLO-affecting symptoms; ticket everything else
Mute the pager overnight so that on-call can sleep properly
Rotate on-call less often so engineers get used to the noise

questions.explanation: Every alert should demand a human action, so alerts that are always ignored should be removed or tuned. Paging only for symptoms that threaten the availability target, and turning lesser issues into tickets for working hours, keeps real pages meaningful.

why_others_wrong.b: More alerts deepen the fatigue and make real problems easier to miss.
why_others_wrong.d: Muting the pager means real overnight outages go unanswered.
why_others_wrong.e: Longer shifts in a noisy rotation make burnout worse.

questions.key_justification: Every page should be actionable and tied to user-facing reliability.

import sys


def error_budget(slo, days):
    """slo: availability target as text with up to 2 decimals, below 100 (like '99.9'). days: list of (requests, failed). The budget is total requests x (100 - slo) / 100 failures. Return (budget rounded down to a whole number, percent of the budget used, True if failures have reached the budget)."""
    whole, _, frac = slo.partition(".")
    slo_bp = int(whole) * 100 + int((frac + "00")[:2])      # '99.9' -> 9990 hundredths of a percent
    total = sum(r for r, _ in days)
    failed = sum(f for _, f in days)
    budget_x10000 = total * (10000 - slo_bp)               # the budget, times 10000, exact
    used_pct = 100 * failed * 10000 / budget_x10000
    return budget_x10000 // 10000, used_pct, failed * 10000 >= budget_x10000


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    slo = data[0].strip()
    n = int(data[1])
    days = [tuple(map(int, data[2 + i].split())) for i in range(n)]
    allowed, used_pct, freeze = error_budget(slo, days)
    print("allowed", allowed)
    print("used", format(used_pct, ".1f") + "%")
    print("status", "FREEZE" if freeze else "OK")


main()
code_pool.explanation: Summing the days gives the month so far; the budget is the failures the SLO allows. Working in hundredths of a percent keeps 99.9 exact (0.1% of 3,000,000 is exactly 3,000). Tying release pace to the remaining budget turns 'move fast versus stay stable' into a number both sides agreed in advance.
code_pool.key_justification: Error budget arithmetic over summed daily counts.

import sys


def group_alerts(alerts, window):
    """alerts: list of (second, alert name) in time order. An alert opens a new incident for its name unless an incident for that name was opened less than `window` seconds earlier; otherwise it joins that incident. Return (total incidents, [(name, raw alerts, incidents)] by raw alerts high to low, ties by name)."""
    opened_at, raw, incidents = {}, {}, {}
    for second, name in alerts:
        raw[name] = raw.get(name, 0) + 1
        if name not in opened_at or second - opened_at[name] >= window:
            opened_at[name] = second                     # a new incident opens
            incidents[name] = incidents.get(name, 0) + 1
    per_name = sorted(((n, raw[n], incidents[n]) for n in raw), key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))
    return sum(incidents.values()), per_name


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    window = int(data[0])
    n = int(data[1])
    alerts = []
    for i in range(n):
        second, name = data[2 + i].split()
        alerts.append((int(second), name))
    total, per_name = group_alerts(alerts, window)
    print("incidents", total)
    for name, raw, incidents in per_name:
        print(name, raw, incidents)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Remembering when each alert name last opened an incident (a dictionary) folds repeats into one incident in a single pass. Ranking names by raw volume shows which alerts generate noise, which are the first candidates to tune, merge or delete.
code_pool.key_justification: Time-window de-duplication keyed by alert name.

scenarios.title: Running Delivery and Incidents at Bharat Bima
scenarios.background: Bharat Bima is a fictional insurance company in Mumbai modernising how its 60 engineers build and run the claims platform. Last month a bad release broke claim submissions for two hours, nobody knew who was in charge during the outage, and the review afterwards ended with one engineer being blamed. Leadership wants a delivery process that is fast, secure and measurable, plus a better way to handle incidents.
constraints: Claims data is regulated and must be protected
Leadership wants measurable improvement within two quarters
Sixty engineers across eight teams share the platform

questions.prompt: Put the steps of handling an outage like last month's in order.

options.text: The commander directs mitigation, such as rolling back the release
Detect the problem from alerts and declare an incident
Hold a blameless postmortem and assign follow-up actions
Name an incident commander and post regular status updates
Confirm that claim submissions have fully recovered

questions.explanation: The incident begins when it is detected and declared, and a named commander then coordinates the response and keeps everyone informed. The team mitigates first, often by rolling back, before digging into the root cause, confirms recovery, and holds the postmortem once the service is stable.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Searching for the root cause before mitigating, which keeps customers unable to submit claims while engineers investigate; restoring service comes first.

questions.key_justification: Detect and declare, coordinate, mitigate, verify recovery, then learn in a postmortem.

questions.prompt: Last month's review blamed one engineer. How should future postmortems be run?

options.text: Find the person responsible and record the mistake in their review
Skip postmortems for any incident that was resolved fairly quickly
Keep them blameless, find system causes, and assign owned actions
Let the most senior person in the room decide the single root cause

questions.explanation: Blameless postmortems assume people acted reasonably with the information and tools they had, so engineers share what really happened. Looking at why the system allowed the failure, such as missing tests or a risky deploy process, produces concrete actions with owners that prevent a repeat.

why_others_wrong.a: Blame makes people hide information, so the real causes stay unfixed.
why_others_wrong.b: Quick incidents still reveal weaknesses that can cause bigger ones later.
why_others_wrong.d: Incidents usually have several contributing causes, and authority is not evidence.

questions.key_justification: Blameless postmortems focus on systemic causes and owned follow-up actions.

questions.prompt: Leadership wants to measure delivery performance. Which set of metrics is widely used for this?

options.text: Lines of code, commits per person, tickets closed and hours worked
Number of servers, CPU usage, disk space and network bandwidth
Story points, meetings attended, test count and pull request count
Deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate and restore time

questions.explanation: The four DORA metrics measure both speed and stability: how often the team deploys, how long a change takes to reach production, what share of changes cause failures, and how quickly service is restored after one. Tracked together, they show whether the team is going faster without breaking more.

why_others_wrong.a: Activity counts reward busyness and are easy to game, not delivery outcomes.
why_others_wrong.b: Infrastructure figures describe machines, not how well software is delivered.
why_others_wrong.c: These measure process activity rather than speed or stability of delivery.

questions.key_justification: The DORA metrics balance delivery speed with stability.

questions.prompt: Claims data is regulated. Which two practices build security into the delivery pipeline?

options.text: Scan dependencies and images for known vulnerabilities in CI
Turn off the security scans whenever the pipeline runs slowly
Keep secrets in a vault and inject them only at runtime
Share one admin deploy token between all eight of the teams
Commit each service's .env file so deploys have every value

questions.explanation: Automated scanning in CI catches known vulnerabilities in libraries and base images before they reach production. A secrets vault keeps credentials out of code and images and delivers them only to the services that need them at runtime.

why_others_wrong.b: Skipping scans to save time lets vulnerable code through exactly when it is easiest to miss.
why_others_wrong.d: One shared admin token cannot be traced to a team and gives every pipeline full power.
why_others_wrong.e: Committed secrets spread to every clone and are very hard to revoke cleanly.

questions.key_justification: Shift security left with automated scans and runtime secret injection.

questions.prompt: Match each goal to the practice that achieves it.

items.text: Every change in production has been reviewed by a second person
Any environment can be recreated from scratch within an hour
Find which service in a chain of calls makes claims slow
Lower the risk carried by each release

targets.text: Small, frequent deploys with feature flags
A protected main branch with required reviews

questions.explanation: A protected branch that requires approved reviews guarantees nothing unreviewed is merged. Infrastructure as code lets environments be rebuilt quickly, distributed tracing follows one request across services to show where time goes, and small, frequent, flagged releases keep each change easy to understand and reverse.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Thinking that bigger, less frequent releases are safer: each one bundles more changes, which makes failures more likely and harder to trace.

questions.key_justification: Reviews, IaC, tracing and small releases each deliver one delivery goal.

code_pool.reference_solution:
import sys


def dora(weeks, deploys, incidents):
    """deploys: one result per deployment, 'ok' or 'fail'. incidents: list of (start minute, end minute). Return (deployments per week, percent of deployments that failed or 0 if none, mean minutes to restore or None if no incidents)."""
    per_week = len(deploys) / weeks
    cfr = 100 * deploys.count("fail") / len(deploys) if deploys else 0.0
    mttr = sum(end - start for start, end in incidents) / len(incidents) if incidents else None
    return per_week, cfr, mttr


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    weeks = int(data[0])
    n = int(data[1])
    deploys = [data[2 + i].split()[1] for i in range(n)]
    m = int(data[2 + n])
    incidents = [tuple(map(int, data[3 + n + i].split())) for i in range(m)]
    per_week, cfr, mttr = dora(weeks, deploys, incidents)
    print("deploys_per_week", format(per_week, ".1f"))
    print("change_failure_rate", format(cfr, ".1f") + "%")
    print("mttr", "-" if mttr is None else format(mttr, ".1f") + " min")


main()
code_pool.explanation: Each metric is a simple ratio over the lists, but the edge cases matter: no deployments must not divide by zero, and no incidents means MTTR is undefined, not 0. Tracking speed (frequency) together with stability (failure rate, restore time) stops a team from improving one by quietly sacrificing the other.
code_pool.key_justification: Aggregate ratios over arrays with safe empty cases.

code_pool.prompt: A database password reached the claims repository last quarter. Add a secret scan to the pipeline. The first line is n, then n added lines from a diff. Complete `scan` and report, in line order (and on one line in this order): `aws_key` for `AKIA` followed by 16 capital letters or digits; `private_key` for a line containing `-----BEGIN` and `PRIVATE KEY-----`; `password` for the word password (any case) followed, after optional spaces, by `=` or `:` and a value that, with spaces and quote marks trimmed, is not empty and does not start with `${`, `os.environ`, `process.env` or `getenv` (those read the secret from the environment, which is fine). The program prints `line N kind` per finding, or CLEAN.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def scan(lines):
    """Return [(line number from 1, kind)] in line order; on one line check aws_key, then private_key, then password. aws_key: 'AKIA' followed by 16 characters that are capital letters or digits. private_key: the line contains '-----BEGIN' and 'PRIVATE KEY-----'. password: 'password' (any case) followed, after optional spaces, by '=' or ':' and a value that, with spaces and quote marks trimmed, is not empty and does not start with '${', 'os.environ', 'process.env' or 'getenv'."""
    # Write your code here.
    return []


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    findings = scan(data[1:1 + n])
    if not findings:
        print("CLEAN")
    for line_no, kind in findings:
        print("line", line_no, kind)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Each rule is a small pattern: a fixed prefix plus a character class and length for AWS keys, fixed markers for key files, and 'password = value' with an allow-list for values read from the environment. Running it on every change stops a secret before it reaches history, where deleting it later no longer helps; a leaked key must be rotated.
code_pool.key_justification: Pattern matching on diff lines (regular expressions).
